Sampled HR@10 measures ranking against the sampled candidate set; it does not establish full-catalog HR@10 superiority. Krichene and Rendle show sampled metrics can reverse model comparisons even in expectation ([paper](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/)). For this benchmark, retain identical users and 99 negatives across trials. Suggested uncertainty analysis: resample users with replacement within each category, preserving each user’s paired baseline–candidate hit indicators; recompute the equally weighted four-category mean difference and report its bootstrap interval alongside category differences. This interval is conditional on the fixed candidates and fitted models; it excludes negative-sampling and training variability. Paired resampling has precedent in retrieval evaluation ([Smucker et al.](https://ciir-publications.cs.umass.edu/getpdf.php?id=885)).

Repeated adaptive validation selection creates optimism: model-selection overfitting can be comparable to reported algorithm gains ([Cawley and Talbot](https://www.jmlr.org/beta/papers/v11/cawley10a.html)). Disclose trial count, search budget and selection rule; label validation intervals exploratory because ordinary bootstrap intervals do not correct winner selection. Leave held-out evaluation to the host. For text attribution, proposed controls—not established findings from these sources—are separately trained, capacity-matched HSTU variants using real text, no text and item-text assignments shuffled within training-frequency bins. Keep each shuffled assignment fixed across training and inference. These controls test whether correct text–item alignment helps beyond added parameters and popularity-related structure; they do not establish causality. Use only permitted titles/descriptions and training-derived popularity. Each control remains one model per category, with no score fusion.
